subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Multitasking Myth
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Multitasking Myth.

hook.text: People who say they're great multitaskers actually perform worse on every task they juggle.

buildup.text: Brain imaging shows that what we call multitasking is really rapid switching between single tasks.

discovery.text: Each switch costs time. It takes roughly half a second for the brain to reconfigure its focus.

twist.text: Heavy multitaskers are worse at filtering distractions than people who rarely multitask.

climax.text: Stanford research found that chronic multitaskers couldn't even identify which task mattered most.

punchline.text: Multitasking isn't a talent—it's a tax.

details.summary: True multitasking on demanding cognitive tasks is essentially impossible. What people call multitasking is actually rapid task switching, which incurs measurable costs in speed, accuracy, and mental energy. Each switch forces the brain to reconfigure its processing, wasting time and effort.
details.whyItMatters: The multitasking myth has enormous practical consequences. Recognizing that switching is costly encourages single-tasking, which is consistently faster and more accurate.
takeaways: Cognitive multitasking is actually rapid task switching
Each switch costs time, accuracy, and mental energy

faq.question: Are there any exceptions where true multitasking works?
faq.answer: Only when one task is fully automatic, like walking while talking. If both tasks require conscious cognitive effort, true simultaneous processing is not possible. Even seemingly simple combinations like listening and reading compete for overlapping brain resources.

faq.question: How much time is lost to task switching?
faq.answer: Research shows each switch can cost 10 to 40 percent of productive time depending on task complexity. Frequent switchers also make more errors and report higher stress levels. The cumulative cost over a workday can amount to hours of lost productivity.
